prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, transforming the analysis of exporting, reallocation across firms and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection moved trade analysis from industries to firms. Melitz (2003) is the single central contribution, and Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI completes the core. Together they explain who exports, why trade liberalisation raises aggregate productivity through reallocation, and why gains from trade operate through a margin that earlier models could not represent. The framework has been tested for more than two decades on firm-level data from many countries. It is textbook material, underpins quantitative trade and policy evaluation, and connects to the reallocation and firm-dynamics literatures in growth. The two-person attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist. A prize for B001 would force a three-name cut from a crowded field of at least eight credited names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum did closely related empirical and quantitative work and are not on this entry. Melitz's contribution is largely one seminal paper, and the welfare conclusions are sensitive to functional-form assumptions such as the Pareto distribution. The committee may also see the work as a continuation of the new-trade-theory line already recognised in 2008. B001 has by far the broadest opening support, and its practical influence on central banking is arguably larger than anything in trade. I do not think diffuse attribution should count against it so heavily that it drops below B021, but that is a real judgement.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B021 only sixth because it overlaps with Krugman's earlier new-trade-theory prize, and he noted that Helpman also appears on another trade ballot. He ranked B002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) first.
responses.response: I take the Krugman overlap seriously but conclude the opposite. Krugman's prize covered increasing returns and monopolistic competition at the industry level. Melitz changes the unit of analysis to the firm and gives a distinct margin, selection and reallocation, with its own empirical content. That is a new discovery rather than a refinement. The Helpman overlap with B044 does not affect this configuration, since B021 credits him for the firm-level work with Melitz and Yeaple, not for protection-for-sale. On B002, the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is clean and foundational, and I rank it below B021 mainly because its empirical grounding is more mixed, a caveat Hassler himself raises. I would not exclude it from consideration.

responses.point: Andersson ranked B001 first and proposed Calvo, Taylor and Woodford, calling Calvo and Taylor the origin points and Woodford the integrator. He treated Redding as a follower rather than a co-originator on B021.
responses.response: I agree on Redding, and it supports a two-person B021. On B001 I qualify my opening view. I had proposed Woodford, Galí and Taylor, but Andersson and others make a good case that Calvo's pricing device and Taylor's contracts are the origin points, and that Galí's work (with Gertler and Clarida) is more an extension and canonisation. I now see Calvo, Taylor and Woodford as the more defensible trio. I still think B001 is harder to attribute than B021. A trio omits Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, each with a strong claim, and Andersson's own note that the credit may be broader than any trio points the same way. That is why I keep it as an alternative rather than as my preferred part.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B021 third. He said Helpman is a natural co-recipient, but that Melitz's contribution is largely one seminal paper, and that quantitative trade models may have superseded part of the framework.
responses.response: Single-paper concentration is common among prize-winning contributions and is not a weakness if the paper reorganised a field, as Melitz (2003) did. On supersession, I read the quantitative trade literature as building on the heterogeneous-firm structure rather than replacing it. The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple margin and the selection mechanism survive inside those models, and the gains-from-trade debate is about how much the margin matters. That is a refinement of the discovery, not a refutation. I accept his point that Bernard, Eaton and Kortum sit just outside the entry, and I flag that below as the main attribution uncertainty.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranked B021 first and called the two-person Helpman-Melitz prize the cleanest attribution. He raised the option of pairing Melitz with Eaton-Kortum-style quantitative work.
responses.response: I agree on the two-person attribution. Pairing with Eaton-Kortum would widen the discovery to a different one, quantitative gains from trade, and Eaton and Kortum are not credited on this entry. I would keep the citation on firm heterogeneity and selection and treat the Eaton-Kortum and Bernard-Jensen lines as acknowledged neighbours rather than additional laureates.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum as co-originators of the firm-level stylised facts and quantitative framework, which would make a Helpman-Melitz prize look incomplete.
Whether the 2008 trade prize is judged to cover this line, so that firm heterogeneity is seen as an extension rather than a distinct step.

Whether B001 deserves priority over B021 given its much broader opening support and larger policy influence, and whether Calvo-Taylor-Woodford or a Galí-inclusive trio is the right attribution if it does.
My assessment rests on general knowledge and the supplied entries and has not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Helpman or Melitz is apparent from my profile, so none affects the preferred configuration. Other connections to disclose, none adjudicated: I have long-running co-authorship with Peter Klenow (B050, ranked last in my opening for that reason); I am an associate professor at IIES, where Torsten Persson (B006) is a colleague, though he is not in my configuration; and I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and John Hassler, who are committee members, not candidates. My own research on firm dynamics and reallocation is close in subject to B021, so I rely on the common criteria.
